concepts.def: White blood cells defend against pathogens.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Diseases & Immunity — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Diseases & Immunity brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Diseases & Immunity.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: T helper cell
Plasma cell
Phagocyte
Memory T cell

mcqs.q: A secondary immune response is faster because of:
options: More antigens
Memory cells
Fewer pathogens
Increased phagocytes

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: ATP is permanent and accumulates with age in cells.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.
Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.

mcqs.q: Where do plants get most of their biomass from?
options: Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.
From carbon dioxide in the air — the carbon in plant tissue comes mostly from CO2 fixed during photosynthesis.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Plants get most of their mass from the soil through their roots.

mcqs.q: Why is ATP described as an 'energy currency' rather than energy storage?
options: Cells store large amounts of ATP for emergency use.
ATP is constantly made and broken down — it transfers energy between reactions rather than storing large amounts for later.
ATP is permanent and accumulates with age in cells.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Memory cell”?
options: Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.
Recognises antigens presented on APCs, releases cytokines to stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.
Y-shaped glycoprotein with variable region complementary to a specific antigen; agglutinates pathogens.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “B cell”?
options: Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen.
Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.
Lymphocyte that, when activated, divides and differentiates into plasma cells producing antibodies.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Antigen”?
options: Recognises antigens presented on APCs, releases cytokines to stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.
Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen.
Lymphocyte that, when activated, divides and differentiates into plasma cells producing antibodies.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Phagocytosis”?
options: Lymphocyte that, when activated, divides and differentiates into plasma cells producing antibodies.
Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.
Y-shaped glycoprotein with variable region complementary to a specific antigen; agglutinates pathogens.
Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Antibody”?
options: Recognises antigens presented on APCs, releases cytokines to stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Y-shaped glycoprotein with variable region complementary to a specific antigen; agglutinates pathogens.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.
Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “T helper cell”?
options: Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen.
Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.
Recognises antigens presented on APCs, releases cytokines to stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Y-shaped glycoprotein with variable region complementary to a specific antigen; agglutinates pathogens.

mcqs.q: After a person recovers from measles they rarely catch it again. Which cells are mainly responsible for this rapid second response?
options: Memory cells
Red blood cells
Platelets
Pathogen cells

mcqs.q: A patient is given an injection of ready-made antibodies to treat a snake bite. This is an example of:
options: Passive immunity
Active immunity from a vaccine
A long-lasting natural immunity
Antibiotic treatment

mcqs.q: A doctor explains that antibiotics will not help a patient's cold. Which is the best reason?
options: Colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill.
Antibiotics only work on the patient's own cells.
The cold virus is already resistant to all antibiotics.
Antibiotics only kill fungi.

mcqs.q: A phagocyte surrounds and engulfs a bacterium. This process is called:
options: Phagocytosis
Photosynthesis
Agglutination
Vaccination

free_texts.q: Type the key term that means: "Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen."
free_texts.hint: It's one of the six key terms above.

sequence.def: Microbe with foreign antigens breaches the body
Phagocyte engulfs and digests the pathogen
Phagocyte displays antigens on its surface
T helper cells bind antigen and release cytokines
Matching B cell divides into plasma and memory cells
Plasma cells secrete antibodies against the antigen
